## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.87055.4.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.87055.4.sa2)

In this work, the authors elaborate on an analytically tractable, continuous-attractor model to study an idealized neural network with realistic spiking phase precession/procession. The key ingredient of this analysis is the inclusion of a mechanism for slow firing-rate adaptation in addition to the otherwise fast continuous-attractor dynamics. The latter continuous-attractor dynamics classically arises from a combination of translation invariance and nonlinear rate normalization.

For strong adaptation/weak external input, the network naturally exhibits an internally generated, travelling-wave dynamics along the attractor with some characteristic speed. For small adaptation/strong external stimulus, the network recovers the classical externally driven continuous-attractor dynamics. Crucially, when both adaptation and external input are moderate, there is a competition with the internally generated and externally generated mechanisms leading to an oscillatory tracking regime. In this tracking regime, the population firing profile oscillates around the neural field tracking the position of the stimulus. The authors demonstrate by a combination of analytical and computational arguments that oscillatory tracking corresponds to realistic phase precession/procession. In particular the authors can account for the emergence of unimodal and bimodal cells, as well as some other experimental observations with respect the dependence of phase precession/procession on the animal's locomotion.

The strengths of this work are at least three-fold: (1) Given its simplicity, the proposed model has a surprisingly large explanatory power of the various experimental observations. (2) The mechanism responsible for the emergence of precession/procession can be understood as a simple yet rather illuminating competition between internally driven and externally driven dynamical trends. (3) Amazingly, and under some adequate simplifying assumptions, a great deal of analysis can be treated exactly, which allows for a detailed understanding of all parametric dependencies. This exact treatment culminates with a full characterization of the phase space of the network dynamics, as well as the computation of various quantities of interest, including characteristic speeds and oscillating frequencies.

As mentioned by the authors themselves, the main limitation of this work is that it deals with a very idealized model and it remains to see how the proposed dynamical behaviors would persists in more realistic models. For example, the model is based on a continuous attractor model that assumes perfect translation-invariance of the network connectivity pattern. Would the oscillating tracking behavior persist in the presence of connection heterogeneities? Another limitation is that the system needs to be tuned to exhibit oscillation within the theta range and that this tuning involves a priori variable parameters such as the external input strength. Is the oscillating-tracking behavior overtly sensitive to input strength variations? The author mentioned that an external pacemaker can serve to drive oscillation within the desired theta band but there is no evidence presented supporting this. A final and perhaps secondary limitation has to do with the choice of parameter, namely the time constant of neural firing which is chosen around 3ms. This seems rather short given that the fast time scale of rate models (excluding synaptic processes) is usually given by the membrane time constant, which is typically about 15ms. I suspect this latter point can easily be addressed.

claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through model simulations with varying adaptation strength.

claims.claim: The intrinsic mobility of the bump dynamics can be understood as neurons around the bump center having the highest firing rates and hence receiving the strongest adaptation, which destabilizes the bump stability at the current location.

Neurons around the bump center have the highest firing rates and hence receive the strongest adaptation. Such strong adaptation destabilizes the bump stability at the current location, and hence pushes the bump away.
claims.evidence: This is an intuitive explanation of the mechanism derived from the model dynamics.

claims.claim: Similar mechanisms have been applied to explain mental exploration, preplay during sharp wave-ripple events in the hippocampus, and the free memory recall phenomenon in the brain.
claims.source: Similar mechanisms have been applied to explain mental exploration (Hopfield, 2010), preplay during sharp wave-ripple events in the hippocampus (Azizi et al., 2013), and the free memory recall phenomenon in the brain (Dong et al., 2021).

claims.claim: The bump oscillation can be well represented as the bump center sweeping around the external input location.
claims.source: Our study shows that during oscillatory tracking, the bump shape is roughly unchanged (see previous sections for the condition of shape variability), and the bump oscillation can be well represented as the bump center sweeping around the external input location.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through model simulations and mathematical analysis.

claims.claim: By setting the parameters appropriately, the bump can oscillate in the theta band (6–10 Hz).
claims.source: By setting the parameters appropriately, the bump can oscillate in the theta band (6–10 Hz), thus approximating the experimentally observed theta sweeps (see below).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through model simulations with appropriate parameter choices.

claims.claim: Theta sweeps are bounded by individual LFP theta cycles in experiments.
claims.source: Notably, LFP theta is not explicitly modeled in the network. However, since theta sweeps are bounded by individual LFP theta cycles in experiments, they share the same oscillation frequency as LFP theta.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: The oscillatory tracking of the bump around the external input naturally gives rise to the forward and backward theta sweeps observed empirically.
claims.source: In our model, the bump center and external input represent the decoded and physical positions of the animal, respectively, thus the oscillatory tracking of the bump around the external input naturally gives rise to the forward and backward theta sweeps observed empirically (Figure 3a and b; Wang et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This connects the model behavior to experimental observations.

claims.claim: When the animal enters the place field, the firing phase of the neuron remains constant, i.e., no phase shift occurs.
claims.source: In summary, oscillatory tracking of the CANN well explains the firing phase shift of place cells when the animal traverses their firing fields. Speciﬁcally, when the animal enters the place field, the firing phase of the neuron remains constant, i.e., no phase shift occurs, which agrees with experimental observations (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Skaggs et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the model that agrees with experimental observations.

claims.claim: As the animal approaches the center of the place field, the firing phase of the neuron starts to shift in two streams, one to earlier phases during the forward sweeps and the other to later phases during the backward sweeps.
claims.source: As the animal approaches the center of the place field, the firing phase of the neuron starts to shift in two streams, one to earlier phases during the forward sweeps and the other to later phases during the backward sweeps.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the model analysis.

claims.claim: When the animal leaves the place field, the firing phase of the neuron stops shifting and remains constant.
claims.source: Finally, when the animal leaves the place field, the firing phase of the neuron stops shifting and remains constant.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the model analysis.

claims.claim: Over the whole process, the firing phase of a place cell is shifted by 180 degrees.
claims.source: Over the whole process, the firing phase of a place cell is shifted by 180 degrees, which agrees with experimental observations (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Skaggs et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the model that agrees with experimental observations.

claims.claim: Bimodal cells exhibit both significant phase precession and procession, which are associated with two firing peaks in a theta cycle.
claims.source: The results above show that during oscillatory tracking, a place cell exhibits both significant phase precession and procession, which are associated with two firing peaks in a theta cycle. These neurons have been described as bimodal cells (Wang et al., 2020; Figure 4a).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through model simulations and connected to experimental observations.

claims.claim: Previous experiments have primarily focused on the phase precession of place cell firing, while tending to ignore phase procession, which is a relatively weaker phenomenon.
claims.source: Conversely, previous experiments have primarily focused on the phase precession of place cell firing, while tending to ignore phase procession, which is a relatively weaker phenomenon (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Skaggs et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of the experimental literature.

claims.claim: When the bump sweeps over a neuron, the delayed adaptation it generates will suppress the bump height as it sweeps back to the same location.
claims.source: This implies that when the bump sweeps over a neuron, the delayed adaptation it generates will suppress the bump height as it sweeps back to the same location.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model dynamics.

claims.claim: Forward sweeps always strongly suppress backward sweeps due to asymmetric suppression effects.
claims.source: Furthermore, since the oscillatory tracking always begins with a forward sweep (as the initial sweep is triggered by the external input moving in the same direction), the suppression effects are asymmetric, i.e., forward sweeps always strongly suppress backward sweeps.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model dynamics.

claims.claim: The bump height in the forward sweep is always higher than that in the backward sweep due to asymmetric suppression.
claims.source: Because of this asymmetric suppression, the bump height in the forward sweep is always higher than that in the backward sweep (see Figure 4c and Appendix 1—figure 3a).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through model simulations shown in Figure 4c.

claims.claim: There is no sharp separation between bimodal and unimodal cells.
claims.source: In summary, different adaptation strengths explain the emergence of bimodal and unimodal cells. In fact, there is no sharp separation between bimodal and unimodal cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model results showing a continuum of behaviors.

claims.claim: As the firing rate adaptation gets stronger, cells with the bimodal firing property will gradually behave more like those with the unimodal firing property.
claims.source: As the firing rate adaptation gets stronger, the network bump is more attenuated during the backward sweep, and cells with the bimodal firing property will gradually behave more like those with the unimodal firing property (see Appendix 1—figure 3b).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through model simulations.

claims.claim: Even though phase procession is weak, it still exists in unimodal cells.
claims.source: Moreover, our model confirms that even though phase procession is weak, it still exists in unimodal cells (Figure 4h, lower panel), which has been reported in previous studies (Wang et al., 2020; Yamaguchi et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through model simulations and supported by experimental citations.

claims.claim: Phase procession is not a characteristic feature of bimodal cells, but instead, is likely a common feature of hippocampal activity, with a strength controlled by adaptation.
claims.source: This implies that phase procession is not a characteristic feature of bimodal cells, but instead, is likely a common feature of hippocampal activity, with a strength controlled by adaptation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claims.claim: Experimental data has indicated that there is a laminar difference between unimodal cells and bimodal cells, with bimodal cells correlating more with the firing patterns of deep CA1 neurons and unimodal cells with the firing patterns of superficial CA1 neurons.
claims.source: Furthermore, the experimental data (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2017) has indicated that there is a laminar difference between unimodal cells and bimodal cells, with bimodal cells correlating more with the firing patterns of deep CA1 neurons and unimodal cells with the firing patterns of superficial CA1 neurons.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental citation.

claims.claim: The laminar difference between unimodal and bimodal cells may come from the different adaptation strengths in the two layers.
claims.source: Our model suggests that this difference may come from the different adaptation strengths in the two layers.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claims.claim: As the animal approaches the choice point in a T-maze, the decoded position from hippocampal activity propagates down one of the two arms alternatively in successive LFP theta cycles.
claims.source: One recent study (Kay et al., 2020) showed constant cycling of theta sweeps in a T-maze environment (Figure 5a), i.e., as the animal approaches the choice point, the decoded position from hippocampal activity propagates down one of the two arms alternatively in successive LFP theta cycles.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental citation.

claims.claim: As the external input approaches the choice point in the T-maze model, the network bump starts to sweep onto left and right arms alternatively in successive theta cycles.
claims.source: As the external input approaches the choice point, the network bump starts to sweep onto left and right arms alternatively in successive theta cycles (Figure 5b and Video 4; see also Romani and Tsodyks, 2015, for a similar model of cyclical sweeps spanning several theta cycles).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through model simulations shown in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: The bump cycling phenomenon gives rise to the 'cycle skipping' effect, where a neuron whose place field is on one of the two arms fires on every other LFP theta cycle before the decision is made.
claims.source: At the single cell level, this bump cycling phenomenon gives rise to the 'cycle skipping' effect (Kay et al., 2020; Deshmukh et al., 2010; Brandon et al., 2013), where a neuron whose place field is on one of the two arms fires on every other LFP theta cycle before the decision is made (Figure 5c, left panel and Figure 5d, upper panel).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through model simulations and connected to experimental observations.

claims.claim: A pair of cells with firing fields on each of the two arms will fire in regular alternation on every other theta cycle.
claims.source: For example, a pair of cells with firing fields on each of the two arms will fire in regular alternation on every other theta cycle (Figure 5c, right panel and Figure 5d, lower panel).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through model simulations shown in Figure 5c and 5d.

claims.claim: The underlying mechanism of constant cycling relies on delayed adaptation, which alternately causes neurons on one arm to be more suppressed than those on the other arm.
claims.source: In summary, our model, extended to a T-maze structure, explains the constant cycling of two possible future scenarios in a T-maze environment. The underlying mechanism relies on delayed adaptation, which alternately causes neurons on one arm to be more suppressed than those on the other arm.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism derived from the model dynamics.

claims.claim: High-speed cycling may contribute to the quick and continuous sampling among multiple future scenarios in real-world decision-making and planning.
claims.source: Such high-speed cycling may contribute to the quick and continuous sampling among multiple future scenarios in real-world decision-making and planning.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of the model behavior.

claims.claim: There is a cyclical effect in the sweep lengths across oscillation cycles before the animal enters the left or right arm.
claims.source: We also note that there is a cyclical effect in the sweep lengths across oscillation cycles before the animal enters the left or right arm (see Figure 5b, lower panel), which may be interesting to check in the experimental data in future work (see Discussion for more details).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the model simulations that could be tested experimentally.

claims.claim: It has been suggested that the theta phase shift provides an additional mechanism to improve the localization of animals.
claims.source: As the firing rate shows large variability when the animal runs through the firing field (Fenton and Muller, 1998), it has been suggested that the theta phase shift provides an additional mechanism to improve the localization of animals (O'Keefe and Burgess, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental and theoretical work.

claims.claim: Taking phase into account leads to a significant improvement in the accuracy of localizing the animal.
claims.source: Indeed, Jensen and Lisman, 2000, showed that taking phase into account leads to a significant improvement in the accuracy of localizing the animal.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to modeling work.

claims.claim: There is a linear relationship between the firing frequency of place cells and the animal's moving speed.
claims.source: To demonstrate the robustness of phase coding, previous experiments showed two intriguing findings: a linear relationship between the ﬁring frequency of place cells and the animal's moving speed (Geisler et al., 2007), and the continued phase shift after interruption of hippocampal activity (Zugaro et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental citation.

claims.claim: There is continued phase shift after interruption of hippocampal activity.
claims.source: To demonstrate the robustness of phase coding, previous experiments showed two intriguing findings: a linear relationship between the ﬁring frequency of place cells and the animal's moving speed (Geisler et al., 2007), and the continued phase shift after interruption of hippocampal activity (Zugaro et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental citation.

claims.claim: The firing frequency of a place cell has a baseline theta frequency, which is the same as the bump oscillation frequency.
claims.source: Therefore, the ﬁring frequency of a place cell has a baseline theta frequency, which is the same as the bump oscillation frequency.
claims.evidence: This is derived from the model analysis.

claims.claim: Due to phase precession, there will be half a cycle more than the baseline theta cycles as the animal runs over the firing field, and hence single-cell oscillatory frequency will be higher than the baseline theta frequency.
claims.source: Furthermore, due to phase precession, there will be half a cycle more than the baseline theta cycles as the animal runs over the ﬁring ﬁeld, and hence single-cell oscillatory frequency will be higher than the baseline theta frequency (Figure 6a).
claims.evidence: This is derived from the model analysis and shown in Figure 6a.

claims.claim: The faster the animal runs, the faster the extra half cycle can be accomplished, and consequently, the firing frequency will increase more than the baseline frequency.
claims.source: The faster the animal runs, the faster the extra half cycle can be accomplished. Consequently, the firing frequency will increase more (a steeper slope in Figure 6a, red dots) than the baseline frequency.
claims.evidence: This is derived from the model analysis and shown in Figure 6a.

claims.claim: The linear relationship between firing frequency and running speed ensures that the firing phase of a unimodal cell in each theta cycle is locked with the relative location of the animal in the firing field of that cell.
claims.source: This linear relationship ensures that the firing phase of a unimodal cell in each theta cycle is locked with the relative location of the animal in the firing field of that cell, which supports a robust phase-position code.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model analysis.

claims.claim: In the model, the speed modulation of the place cells' firing frequency is not the cause of theta phase shift, but rather a result of oscillatory tracking.
claims.source: Notably, in our model, the speed modulation of the place cells' firing frequency is not the cause of theta phase shift, but rather a result of oscillatory tracking.
claims.evidence: This distinguishes the mechanism in this model from other models.

claims.claim: This is different from the dual oscillator model, which assumes that phase precession is caused by a speed-dependent increase in the dendritic oscillation frequency.
claims.source: This is different from the dual oscillator model (Lengyel et al., 2003), which assumes that phase precession is caused by a speed-dependent increase in the dendritic oscillation frequency (see Discussion for more details).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to another model in the literature.

claims.claim: The firing phase of a place cell continues to precess even after hippocampal activity was transiently silenced for up to 250 ms.
claims.source: In a different experiment, Zugaro et al., 2005, found that the firing phase of a place cell continues to precess even after hippocampal activity was transiently silenced for up to 250 ms (around 2 theta cycles).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental citation.

claims.claim: No matter how long the network is inactivated, the new firing phase will only be determined by the new location of the animal in the place field.
claims.source: This means that the firing phase keeps tracking the animal's physical location. No matter how long the network is inactivated, the new firing phase will only be determined by the new location of the animal in the place field.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model analysis.

claims.claim: The firing phase in the first bump oscillation cycle after the network perturbation is more advanced than the firing phase in the last bump oscillation cycle right before the perturbation, and the amount of precession is similar to that in the case without perturbation.
claims.source: Therefore, the firing phase in the first bump oscillation cycle after the network perturbation is more advanced than the firing phase in the last bump oscillation cycle right before the perturbation, and the amount of precession is similar to that in the case without perturbation (Figure 6c).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through model simulations shown in Figure 6c.

claims.claim: There exists a one-to-one correspondence between the firing phase of a place cell and the traveled distance in the neuron's place field, which is independent of the animal's running speed or the perturbation duration.
claims.source: Overall, our model reproduces these two experimental findings, and suggests that there exists a one-to-one correspondence between the firing phase of a place cell and the traveled distance in the neuron's place field, which is independent of the animal's running speed or the perturbation duration (Appendix 1—figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the model analysis.

claims.claim: Theta phase correlates better with the animal's location than with time.
claims.source: This agrees well with experimental observations (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993) that theta phase correlates better with the animal's location than with time (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental citation and model results.

claims.claim: A bimodal cell will have two peaks in its firing frequency, with one slightly higher than the LFP theta baseline (due to phase precession) and the other slightly lower than the LFP theta baseline (due to phase procession).
claims.source: First, in contrast to a unimodal cell, a bimodal cell will have two peaks in its firing frequency, with one slightly higher than the LFP theta baseline (due to phase precession) and the other slightly lower than the LFP theta baseline (due to phase procession).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claims.claim: The precession-associated frequency positively correlates with the running speed of the animal, while the procession-associated frequency negatively correlates with the running speed.
claims.source: The precession-associated frequency positively correlates with the running speed of the animal, while the procession-associated frequency negatively correlates with the running speed (Figure 6b).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the model shown in Figure 6b.

claims.claim: Both the phase precession and procession of a bimodal cell after transient intrahippocampal perturbation continue from the new location of the animal, no matter how long the silencing period lasts.
claims.source: Second, similar to the preserved phase shift in unimodal cells, both the phase precession and procession of a bimodal cell after transient intrahippocampal perturbation continue from the new location of the animal (see Appendix 1—figure 5), no matter how long the silencing period lasts.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claims.claim: Oscillatory tracking has been studied previously in an excitatory-inhibitory neural network.
claims.source: As a subject of network dynamics, oscillatory tracking has been studied previously in an excitatory-inhibitory neural network (Folias and Bressloff, 2004), where it was found that decreasing the external input strength can lead to periodic emission of traveling waves in the network (Hopf instability), which is analogous to the oscillatory tracking state in our model.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous modeling work.

claims.claim: The oscillatory interference model produces phase precession via the superposition of two oscillatory signals, with one from the baseline somatic oscillation at the LFP theta frequency and the other from the dendritic oscillation whose frequency is slightly higher.
claims.source: A representative example of the former is the oscillatory interference model (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Lengyel et al., 2003), which produces phase precession via the superposition of two oscillatory signals, with one from the baseline somatic oscillation at the LFP theta frequency (reﬂecting the inputs from the medial septal pacemaker; Stewart and Fox, 1990), and the other from the dendritic oscillation whose frequency is slightly higher.
claims.evidence: This is a description of another model in the literature.

claims.claim: It remains unclear how oscillation of individual neurons has a frequency higher than the baseline theta frequency in the oscillatory interference model.
claims.source: While these models can explain a large variety of experimental phenomena, it remain unclear how oscillation of individual neurons has a frequency higher than the baseline theta frequency.
claims.evidence: This identifies a limitation of previous models.

claims.claim: The current model provides a network mechanism for how higher-frequency oscillation emerges.
claims.source: Here, our model provides a network mechanism for how such higher-frequency oscillation emerges.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of the current model.

claims.claim: The activation spreading model produces phase precession via the propagation of neural activity along the movement direction, which relies on asymmetric synaptic connections.
claims.source: A representative model relying on neuronal recurrent interactions is the activation spreading model (Tsodyks et al., 1996). This model produces phase precession via the propagation of neural activity along the movement direction, which relies on asymmetric synaptic connections.
claims.evidence: This is a description of another model in the literature.

claims.claim: A later version of the activation spreading model considers short-term synaptic plasticity (short-term depression) to implicitly implement asymmetric connections between place cells.
claims.source: A later version of this model considers short-term synaptic plasticity (short-term depression) to implicitly implement asymmetric connections between place cells (Romani and Tsodyks, 2015), and reproduces many other interesting phenomena, such as phase precession in different environments.
claims.evidence: This is a description of another model in the literature.

claims.claim: The current model considers firing rate adaptation to implement symmetry breaking and hence generates activity propagation.
claims.source: Different from these two models, our model considers firing rate adaptation to implement symmetry breaking and hence generates activity propagation.
claims.evidence: This distinguishes the mechanism in the current model from previous models.

claims.claim: In the activation spreading model, an external theta input is considered to reset the bump location at the end of each theta cycle.
claims.source: To prevent the activity bump from spreading away, their model considers an external theta input to reset the bump location at the end of each theta cycle, whereas our model generates an internal oscillatory state, where the activity bump travels back due to the attraction of external location input once it spreads too far away.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the mechanism in another model.

claims.claim: The current model generates an internal oscillatory state, where the activity bump travels back due to the attraction of external location input once it spreads too far away.
claims.source: To prevent the activity bump from spreading away, their model considers an external theta input to reset the bump location at the end of each theta cycle, whereas our model generates an internal oscillatory state, where the activity bump travels back due to the attraction of external location input once it spreads too far away.
claims.evidence: This distinguishes the mechanism in the current model from previous models.

claims.claim: Both STD and SFA show the ability to produce bi-directional sweeps within a CANN model.
claims.source: Based on our simulation, both STD and SFA show the ability to produce bi-directional sweeps within a CANN model, with the SFA uniquely enabling uni-directional sweeps in the absence of external theta inputs.
claims.evidence: This is based on simulation results comparing different mechanisms.

claims.claim: SFA uniquely enables uni-directional sweeps in the absence of external theta inputs.
claims.source: Based on our simulation, both STD and SFA show the ability to produce bi-directional sweeps within a CANN model, with the SFA uniquely enabling uni-directional sweeps in the absence of external theta inputs.
claims.evidence: This is based on simulation results comparing different mechanisms.

claims.claim: STD attenuates the neural activity through a reduction in recurrent connection strength, whereas SFA provides inhibitory input directly to the neurons.
claims.source: Specifically, STD attenuates the neural activity through a reduction in recurrent connection strength, whereas SFA provides inhibitory input directly to the neurons, potentially impacting all excitatory inputs.
claims.evidence: This describes the mechanistic differences between STD and SFA.

claims.claim: The mechanism of generating theta sweeps proposed in the model can be generalized to more complex environments beyond the linear track.
claims.source: Besides the linear track environment, the mechanism of generating theta sweeps proposed in our model can also be generalized to more complex environments.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the generalizability of the model.

claims.claim: In a previous model, the network activity propagates continuously from the current location on the center arm till the end of the outer arm, which takes a few theta cycles.
claims.source: Similar alternative activity sweeps in the T-maze environment has been studied in a previous paper (Romani and Tsodyks, 2015), which showed that the frequency of alternation correlates with overtly deliberative behaviors such as head scans (frequency at 1 Hz or less) (Johnson and Redish, 2007). In contrast to our model, the network activity in their model propagates continuously from the current location on the center arm till the end of the outer arm, which takes a few theta cycles (i.e. 1 s or more).
claims.evidence: This is a description of another model in the literature.

claims.claim: In the current model, the network bump alternately sweeps to one of the two outer arms at a much higher frequency (∼ 8 Hz).
claims.source: In our model, the network bump alternately sweeps to one of the two outer arms at a much higher frequency (∼ 8 Hz), which may be related to fast decision-making or planing in natural environments (Kay et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the model simulations.

claims.claim: The model can be easily extended to the multiple-arms (>2) environment or the cascade-T environment with the underlying mechanism of generating theta cycling remaining unchanged.
claims.source: Furthermore, our model can also be easily extended to the multiple-arms (>2) environment (Gillespie et al., 2021) or the cascade-T environment (Johnson and Redish, 2007) with the underlying mechanism of generating theta cycling remaining unchanged.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the extensibility of the model.

claims.claim: Phase shift has been reported when an animal navigates in an open field environment.
claims.source: In addition to the linear and T-maze environments, phase shift has also been reported when an animal navigates in an open field environment.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about experimental observations.

claims.claim: Due to the lack of recorded neurons, decoding theta sweeps in the 2D environment is not as straightforward as in the 1D case.
claims.source: However, due to the lack of recorded neurons, decoding theta sweeps in the 2D environment is not as straightforward as in the 1D case.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about experimental limitations.

claims.claim: In the 2D CANN, the activity bump will sweep along the tangent direction of the movement trajectory, similar to the 1D case.
claims.source: Our preliminary result shows that in the 2D CANN where neurons are arranged homogeneously according to their relative firing locations, the activity bump will sweep along the tangent direction of the movement trajectory, similar to the 1D case (see 'Oscillatory tracking in the 2D CANN – modeling theta sweeps in the open ﬁeld environment' and Appendix 1—figure 6 for details).
claims.evidence: This is a preliminary result from model simulations.

claims.claim: The height of the activity bump in the forward sweep window is higher than that in the backward sweep window due to the asymmetric suppression effect from the adaptation.
claims.source: For instance, the height of the activity bump in the forward sweep window is higher than that in the backward sweep window (Figure 4c) due to the asymmetric suppression effect from the adaptation.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the model shown in Figure 4c.

claims.claim: For bimodal cells, they will have two peaks in their firing frequency as the animal runs across the firing fields, with one corresponding to phase precession and the other corresponding to phase procession.
claims.source: For bimodal cells, they will have two peaks in their firing frequency as the animal runs across the firing ﬁelds, with one corresponding to phase precession and the other corresponding to phase procession.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claims.claim: As the animal runs toward the decision point in the T-maze, the theta sweep length shows cyclical patterns.
claims.source: Interestingly, our model of the T-maze environment showed an expected phenomenon that as the animal runs toward the decision point, the theta sweep length also shows cyclical patterns (Figure 5b, lower panel).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the model simulations shown in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: The model can be easily extended to the grid cell population without changing the underlying mechanism.
claims.source: In the current study, we have modeled the place cell population in the hippocampus with a CANN and adopted firing rate adaptation to generate theta phase shift. In fact, this model can be easily extended to the grid cell population without changing the underlying mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the extensibility of the model.

claims.claim: Neurons in the grid cell network will exhibit phase shift as the animal moves through the grid field.
claims.source: For instance, we can induce the torus-like connection profile (periodic boundary in the 2D space) (Samsonovich and McNaughton, 1997; McNaughton et al., 2006) or the locally inhibitory connection profile (Burak and Fiete, 2009; Couey et al., 2013) in the CANN structure to construct a grid cell model, and by imposing firing rate adaptation, neurons in the grid cell network will also exhibit phase shift as the animal moves through the grid field, as reported in previous experimental studies (Hafting et al., 2008; van der Meer and Redish, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from extending the model to grid cells, supported by experimental citations.

claims.claim: Grid cells and place cells might be coordinated by the same external input from the environment, as well as by the medial septum which is known to be a pacemaker that synchronizes theta oscillations across different brain regions.
claims.source: Notably, although for both grid cells and place cells, CANNs can generate theta phase shift, it does not mean that they are independent from each other. Instead, they might be coordinated by the same external input from the environment, as well as by the medial septum which is known to be a pacemaker that synchronizes theta oscillations across different brain regions (King et al., 1998; Wang, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis about coordination mechanisms, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The 'online' theta sweep and the 'offline' replay may share some common features in their underlying mechanisms.
claims.source: Our model also suggests that the 'online' theta sweep and the 'offline' replay may share some common features in their underlying mechanisms (Romani and Tsodyks, 2015; Hopfield, 2010; Kang and DeWeese, 2019; Jahnke et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to related work.

claims.claim: The activity bump with strong adaptation can move spontaneously when the external input becomes weak enough.
claims.source: We have shown that the activity bump with strong adaptation can move spontaneously when the external input becomes weak enough (see previous sections).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the model analysis.

claims.claim: Non-local spreading of neural activity has a speed much faster than the conventional speed of animals, which resembles the fast spreading of the decoded position during sharp wave-ripple events.
claims.source: Such non-local spreading of neural activity has a speed much faster than the conventional speed of animals (the external input speed in our model, see Figure 2d), which resembles the fast spreading of the decoded position during sharp wave-ripple events (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011).
claims.evidence: This connects the model behavior to experimental observations of replay.

claims.claim: Theta sweeps originate from the interplay between the adaptation and the external input, while replay originates from only the adaptation, since the external input is relatively weak during the 'offline' state.
claims.source: This indicates that these two phenomena may be generated by the same neural mechanism of firing rate adaptation, with theta sweeps originating from the interplay between the adaptation and the external input, while replay originating from only the adaptation, since the external input is relatively weak during the 'offline' state.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis about the relationship between theta sweeps and replay.

claims.claim: The coordinated emergence of theta sequences and replays during the post-natal development period supports the hypothesis that they share the same neural mechanism.
claims.source: This hypothesis seems to be supported by the coordinated emergence of theta sequences and replays during the post-natal development period (Muessig et al., 2019), as well as their simultaneous degradation when the animal traveled passively on a model train (Drieu et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental citations.

claims.claim: The CANN adopted in the current study is an idealized model for the place cell population, where many biological details are missed.
claims.source: Nevertheless, it is important to note that the CANN we adopt in the current study is an idealized model for the place cell population, where many biological details are missed (Amari, 1977; Tsodyks and Sejnowski, 1995; Samsonovich and McNaughton, 1997; Tsodyks, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of model limitations.

claims.claim: The translation-invariant connection pattern may be learned by a synaptic plasticity rule at the behavioral timescale when the animal navigates actively in the environment.
claims.source: For instance, we have assumed that neuronal synaptic connections are translation-invariant in the space. In practice, such a connection pattern may be learned by a synaptic plasticity rule at the behavioral timescale when the animal navigates actively in the environment (Bittner et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis about how the connection pattern could be implemented, supported by citation.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the background that hippocampal place cells exhibit theta phase precession and procession during locomotion, which are thought to support cognitive functions including planning and memory. However, the neural mechanisms underlying these phenomena, particularly interleaved forward and reverse sequences, remain largely unknown.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately characterize the established experimental literature and identify a genuine gap in understanding. The claims are well-supported by appropriate citations to experimental work (O'Keefe and Recce 1993, Skaggs et al. 1996, Wang et al. 2020) and represent accepted knowledge in the field. This provides appropriate motivation for the modeling study.

results.result: The authors develop a continuous attractor neural network (CANN) model where firing rate adaptation destabilizes bump attractor states, creating intrinsic mobility. When adaptation is strong enough, the network bump can travel spontaneously, and under competition between intrinsic and extrinsic (sensory input-driven) mobility, the network displays an oscillatory tracking state where the bump sweeps back and forth around external input.
results.evaluation: The model architecture and dynamics are clearly described with mathematical formulations (Equations 1-13) and demonstrated through simulations (Figure 2). The theoretical analysis of bump stability, intrinsic mobility conditions (m > τ/τ_v), and oscillatory tracking regimes is mathematically derived and validated by simulations showing agreement between theory and simulation (Figure 2h,i). The mechanism is well-explained.

results.result: The oscillatory tracking state of the CANN naturally reproduces theta sweeps observed in hippocampus, where decoded position oscillates around the animal's physical location at theta frequency (6-10 Hz). The model generates forward and backward sweeps that resemble experimental observations.
results.evaluation: The connection between model dynamics and experimental theta sweeps is demonstrated through simulations (Figure 3a,b) that qualitatively match experimental data patterns. The oscillation frequency can be tuned to theta range through parameter selection, and the model reproduces the key phenomenology of theta sweeps. However, the model does not explicitly generate LFP theta but assumes correspondence based on experimental observations.

results.result: Forward sweeps of the network bump account for theta phase precession while backward sweeps account for theta phase procession of individual place cells. As an animal traverses a place field, firing phase remains constant upon entry, shifts in two streams (earlier for forward sweeps, later for backward sweeps) near the field center, and remains constant upon exit, with total phase shift of 180 degrees.
results.evaluation: The phase shift mechanism is derived analytically (Equation 7) and demonstrated through simulations (Figure 3c-e). The model correctly predicts the 180-degree total phase shift and the three-stage progression through the place field, matching experimental observations (O'Keefe and Recce 1993, Skaggs et al. 1996). The mathematical analysis clearly links bump position dynamics to firing phase.

results.result: Varying adaptation strength explains the difference between bimodal cells (showing interleaved phase precession and procession with two firing peaks per theta cycle) and unimodal cells (showing predominant phase precession with one peak). Strong adaptation causes asymmetric suppression where forward sweeps suppress backward sweeps, creating a continuum from bimodal to unimodal behavior.
results.evaluation: The mechanism is clearly demonstrated through simulations showing how increasing adaptation strength progressively attenuates backward sweep amplitude (Figure 4c,d). The model reproduces both bimodal and unimodal firing patterns (Figure 4a,b,g,h) and explains weak phase procession in unimodal cells, consistent with experimental observations (Wang et al. 2020, Yamaguchi et al. 2002). The asymmetric suppression mechanism is well-explained.

results.result: The model extended to T-maze geometry reproduces constant cycling of theta sweeps between left and right arms at ~8 Hz as the animal approaches the choice point. This generates 'cycle skipping' where neurons fire on alternating theta cycles, with the mechanism relying on delayed adaptation alternately suppressing neurons on each arm.
results.evaluation: The T-maze simulations (Figure 5b) clearly demonstrate alternating sweeps onto left and right arms, reproducing the cycle skipping phenomenon observed experimentally (Kay et al. 2020). The auto-correlogram and cross-correlogram analyses (Figure 5d) match experimental patterns. The delayed adaptation mechanism provides a clear explanation for the alternation. The cyclical sweep length pattern is noted as a testable prediction.

results.result: The model explains the linear relationship between place cell firing frequency and running speed. Firing frequency has a baseline theta component plus an additional half-cycle due to phase precession, with faster running speeds completing this extra cycle faster, resulting in higher frequencies. This differs from dual oscillator models where speed modulation causes phase shift.
results.evaluation: The frequency-speed relationship is demonstrated through simulations (Figure 6a) and explained mechanistically. The model correctly predicts that firing frequency increases linearly with speed, matching experimental observations (Geisler et al. 2007). The distinction from dual oscillator models is clearly articulated - in this model, speed modulation is a consequence rather than cause of phase shift. The mechanism is internally consistent.

results.result: The model reproduces continued phase shift after transient hippocampal silencing (up to 250 ms), with firing phase determined by the animal's new location in the place field regardless of silencing duration. This demonstrates a one-to-one correspondence between firing phase and traveled distance, independent of speed or perturbation duration.
results.evaluation: The silencing experiment is simulated (Figure 6c) and shows that phase shift continues from the new location after perturbation, matching experimental observations (Zugaro et al. 2005). The mechanism - that phase is determined by relative position in the place field rather than time - is clearly explained and demonstrated. This supports robust phase-position coding and agrees with experimental findings that phase correlates better with location than time.

results.result: The model suggests that laminar differences between unimodal and bimodal cells (superficial vs. deep CA1 neurons) may arise from different adaptation strengths in the two layers.
results.evaluation: While the model provides a plausible mechanistic explanation for observed laminar differences (Fernández-Ruiz et al. 2017), this is presented as a suggestion without direct experimental validation or specific predictions about adaptation strength differences between layers. The claim is speculative and would require experimental measurement of adaptation properties in different CA1 layers to be supported.

results.result: The model makes several testable predictions for bimodal cells: two peaks in firing frequency (one above and one below theta baseline), with precession-associated frequency positively correlated with speed and procession-associated frequency negatively correlated; continued phase shift after perturbation; and higher bump height in forward vs. backward sweeps.
results.evaluation: These predictions follow logically from the model's mechanisms and are demonstrated in simulations (Figure 6b, Figure 4c, Appendix figures). The predictions are specific and testable, though they have not yet been experimentally validated. The asymmetric suppression mechanism clearly predicts differential bump heights, and the frequency predictions follow from the phase shift dynamics.

results.result: The model provides a network mechanism for higher-frequency oscillation in place cells, addressing a limitation of oscillatory interference models. Unlike activation spreading models that require external theta reset, this model generates internal oscillatory states through firing rate adaptation rather than asymmetric connections or short-term depression.
results.evaluation: The comparison to existing models is fair and well-documented with appropriate citations. The model's novel contribution - using firing rate adaptation to generate oscillatory tracking without external theta reset - is clearly articulated and demonstrated. The distinction from both oscillatory interference models (O'Keefe and Recce 1993, Lengyel et al. 2003) and activation spreading models (Tsodyks et al. 1996, Romani and Tsodyks 2015) is substantive.

results.result: Both short-term depression (STD) and spike frequency adaptation (SFA) can produce bi-directional sweeps in the CANN model, but SFA uniquely enables uni-directional sweeps without external theta inputs. The mechanisms differ in that STD reduces recurrent connection strength while SFA provides direct inhibitory input to neurons.
results.evaluation: The comparison between STD and SFA mechanisms is based on simulations and the mechanistic differences are clearly explained. However, the claim that the difference in uni-directional sweep capability might be due to incomplete parameter exploration is appropriately acknowledged. The mechanistic distinction between the two forms of adaptation is valid.

results.result: The model can be generalized beyond linear tracks to complex environments including T-mazes (demonstrated), multiple-arm mazes, cascade-T environments, and 2D open fields. Preliminary 2D results show sweeps along the tangent direction of movement trajectories.
results.evaluation: The T-maze extension is fully demonstrated with simulations. The claims about other environments are reasonable extrapolations given the model's structure, though not all are fully implemented. The 2D preliminary results (Appendix 1-figure 6) support the claim about tangent direction sweeps. The generalizability claims are appropriately qualified as extensions or preliminary results.

results.result: The model can be extended to grid cells by modifying the connection profile (torus-like or locally inhibitory), and grid cells would exhibit phase shift as animals move through grid fields. Grid cells and place cells might be coordinated by common external input and medial septum pacemaker signals.
results.evaluation: While the extension to grid cells is plausible given the model architecture and is supported by experimental observations of grid cell phase precession (Hafting et al. 2008, van der Meer and Redish 2011), this is presented as a future direction without actual implementation or simulation. The coordination hypothesis is speculative, though supported by relevant citations about medial septum function.

results.result: The model suggests that online theta sweeps and offline replay may share common mechanisms based on firing rate adaptation. Theta sweeps arise from interplay between adaptation and external input, while replay arises from adaptation alone when external input is weak. The spontaneous bump movement speed during strong adaptation resembles fast replay speeds.
results.evaluation: While the model demonstrates that strong adaptation can produce spontaneous bump movement at speeds faster than typical locomotion (Figure 2d), resembling replay, the connection between theta sweeps and replay remains speculative. The supporting evidence from coordinated development (Muessig et al. 2019) and simultaneous degradation (Drieu et al. 2018) is correlational. The hypothesis is plausible but requires further modeling and experimental validation.

results.result: The CANN model is acknowledged as idealized, missing many biological details. The translation-invariant connection pattern assumed in the model may be learned through synaptic plasticity during active navigation.
results.evaluation: The authors appropriately acknowledge model limitations and the idealized nature of the CANN framework. The suggestion about learning connection patterns through plasticity (Bittner et al. 2017) is reasonable but speculative. This represents appropriate scientific caution about model assumptions.

results.result: Theta phase shift provides an additional mechanism to improve animal localization beyond firing rate, which shows large variability. Taking phase into account significantly improves localization accuracy.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately represent prior work (Fenton and Muller 1998, O'Keefe and Burgess 2005, Jensen and Lisman 2000) and provide appropriate context for the functional significance of the phenomena being modeled. The claims are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: The model predicts cyclical patterns in theta sweep length as the animal approaches the T-maze decision point, with alternating long and short sweeps due to delayed adaptation effects.
results.evaluation: This prediction is clearly demonstrated in simulations (Figure 5b, lower panel) and a mechanistic explanation is provided based on the slow dynamics of adaptation. The prediction is specific and testable, though not yet experimentally validated. The authors appropriately note this as something to check in future experimental data.

results.result: The model demonstrates that firing rate adaptation in a continuous attractor neural network produces oscillatory tracking, where the activity bump oscillates around external input. This generates forward and backward sweeps that naturally account for theta phase precession and procession of individual neurons, explaining experimentally observed theta sweeps.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly support this as the main result. The editor states it provides 'valuable new insights' with 'convincing evidence.' Reviewer 1 calls findings (1) and (2) (forward and backward sequences) 'the main result of the paper' that is 'likely to be of interest.' Reviewer 2 describes the model as having 'surprisingly large explanatory power' and praises the 'simple yet rather illuminating competition between internally driven and externally driven dynamical trends.'

results.result: By tuning adaptation strength, the model explains the difference between bimodal cells (showing interleaved phase precession and procession with two firing peaks per theta cycle) and unimodal cells (where phase precession predominates). There is a continuum between these cell types controlled by adaptation strength.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly lists this among predictions 'especially interesting to experimentalists' starting at line 366. Reviewer 2 states 'the authors can account for the emergence of unimodal and bimodal cells' as part of the model's strengths. No reviewer challenges this finding, and it is presented as a natural consequence of the oscillatory tracking mechanism.

results.result: The model explains constant cycling of theta sweeps in a T-maze environment, where the decoded position alternately propagates down different arms in successive theta cycles. This produces 'cycle skipping' effects at the single-cell level and cyclical patterns in sweep lengths.
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly mentions 'constant cycling of sweeps across different arms of a T-maze' as a key insight. Reviewer 1 acknowledges the authors 'give credit for showing how this constant cycling can occur across individual theta cycles,' though notes similarity to Romani & Tsodyks 2015. Reviewer 1 also asks about the cyclical sweep length pattern (Fig 5b), suggesting it should be 'remarked upon and included in the discussion,' indicating acceptance of the phenomenon.

results.result: The model explains speed modulation of place cell firing frequency, showing a linear relationship between firing frequency and running speed. This emerges as a consequence of oscillatory tracking rather than being the cause of phase shift, distinguishing it from dual oscillator models.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'the section on the speed dependence of theta (starting with line 327) was very hard to understand' and requests 'a more graphical explanation of the phenomenon.' This indicates the reviewer accepts the result exists but finds the explanation unclear. The reviewer does not challenge the validity of the finding itself, only its presentation.

results.result: The model reproduces continued phase shift after transient hippocampal silencing, showing that firing phase tracks the animal's physical location independent of perturbation duration. This demonstrates a one-to-one correspondence between firing phase and traveled distance.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 expresses difficulty understanding this result: 'I had a hard time understanding how the Zugaro et al., (2005) hippocampal inactivation experiment was accounted for by the model.' The reviewer's intuition suggests 'there is nothing to keep track of where the bump should be when the activity comes back on line' and requests more explanation. This indicates uncertainty about the mechanism rather than rejection of the claim.

results.result: When adaptation is strong enough, the network bump can travel spontaneously in the attractor space (intrinsic mobility). This occurs because neurons at the bump center receive the strongest adaptation, destabilizing the bump at its current location.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly describes this as a key strength: 'For strong adaptation/weak external input, the network naturally exhibits an internally generated, travelling-wave dynamics along the attractor with some characteristic speed.' This is presented as part of the model's three-fold strengths and is not challenged by any reviewer.

results.result: Due to delayed adaptation and asymmetric suppression effects, the bump height in forward sweeps is always higher than in backward sweeps. Forward sweeps always strongly suppress backward sweeps because oscillatory tracking begins with a forward sweep.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly lists this as 'a prediction that the bump height in the forward direction should be higher than in the backward direction' among predictions that 'would be especially interesting to experimentalists.' The reviewer requests these be 'listed more prominently in a separate section in the discussion,' indicating acceptance of the finding.

results.result: The model predicts that bimodal cells will have two peaks in firing frequency (one above and one below LFP theta baseline), with precession-associated frequency positively correlating with running speed and procession-associated frequency negatively correlating. Both phase precession and procession continue after hippocampal perturbation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly includes 'predictions about bimodal and unimodal cells starting with line 366' among predictions that should be listed prominently for experimentalists. No reviewer challenges these predictions, treating them as natural extensions of the model's core mechanisms.

results.result: Both short-term depression (STD) and spike frequency adaptation (SFA) can produce bi-directional sweeps within a CANN model, but SFA uniquely enables uni-directional sweeps without external theta inputs. STD and SFA differ mechanistically in how they attenuate neural activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 challenges an 'unsubstantiated claim in the paragraph beginning with line 413 that the Tsodyks and Romani (2015) model could not account for forwards and backwards sweeps,' stating 'it is far from obvious to me that both forward and backward sweeps are not possible in the Tsodyks and Romani model.' The reviewer demands the authors 'either prove that this is the case (with theory or simulation) or excise this statement.' This indicates uncertainty about the claimed distinction.

results.result: In a 2D CANN model, the activity bump sweeps along the tangent direction of the movement trajectory, similar to the 1D case, extending the mechanism to open field environments.
results.evaluation: This is presented as a preliminary result and no reviewer challenges it. The claim is modest (extending to 2D) and follows naturally from the 1D mechanism. The lack of reviewer comment suggests implicit acceptance of this straightforward extension.

results.result: The model suggests that online theta sweeps and offline replay may share common mechanisms based on firing rate adaptation. Theta sweeps arise from interplay between adaptation and external input, while replay arises from adaptation alone when external input is weak.
results.evaluation: No reviewer challenges this hypothesis. It is presented as a natural extension of the model's core mechanism, and the authors provide experimental citations supporting coordinated emergence of theta sequences and replays. The lack of reviewer critique suggests acceptance of this as a reasonable speculation.

results.result: By setting parameters appropriately, the bump can oscillate in the theta band (6-10 Hz). While LFP theta is not explicitly modeled, theta sweeps share the same oscillation frequency as LFP theta because they are bounded by individual LFP theta cycles experimentally.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises concerns about model tuning: 'the system needs to be tuned to exhibit oscillation within the theta range and that this tuning involves a priori variable parameters such as the external input strength. Is the oscillating-tracking behavior overtly sensitive to input strength variations?' The reviewer also notes 'The author mentioned that an external pacemaker can serve to drive oscillation within the desired theta band but there is no evidence presented supporting this.' This indicates uncertainty about the robustness of theta-frequency oscillations.

results.result: The CANN is an idealized model where many biological details are missing, including the assumption of translation-invariant connections. Such connection patterns may be learned through synaptic plasticity during active navigation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly raises this as 'the main limitation of this work is that it deals with a very idealized model' and questions 'Would the oscillating tracking behavior persist in the presence of connection heterogeneities?' This is presented as a limitation acknowledged by the authors themselves. The reviewer expresses uncertainty about whether the behavior would persist in more realistic models.

comparisons.comparison: Both address the hippocampal inactivation experiment (C12, C77, C84, C86-C89). OpenEval finds the mechanism well-explained and supported by simulations. Peer reviewer expresses difficulty understanding how the model accounts for this experiment, indicating uncertainty about the mechanism rather than rejecting it.

Both evaluate the comparison between STD and SFA mechanisms (C102-C104). OpenEval finds the mechanistic distinction valid and supported. Peer reviewer challenges the claim that Tsodyks & Romani 2015 model cannot produce bidirectional sweeps, demanding proof or removal of the statement, indicating uncertainty about this distinction.

Both address the connection between theta sweeps and replay (C118-C122). OpenEval rates this as uncertain, noting it's speculative and requires further validation. Peer reviewer supports this as a reasonable speculation with no challenges, suggesting acceptance of the hypothesis.

Both evaluate model limitations and idealized assumptions (C123-C124). OpenEval supports the authors' acknowledgment of limitations as appropriate scientific caution. Peer reviewer expresses uncertainty about whether behavior would persist in more realistic models, viewing idealization as the main limitation.

Both address T-maze cycle skipping and alternating sweeps (C10, C67-C71, C73). OpenEval finds this clearly demonstrated and well-explained. Peer reviewer also supports this finding, with the editor highlighting it as a key insight, though noting similarity to prior work.

Both evaluate frequency-speed relationship (C11, C76, C78-C82). OpenEval finds the mechanism well-demonstrated and internally consistent. Peer reviewer finds the result hard to understand and requests better graphical explanation, indicating acceptance of the finding but difficulty with presentation.

Both address predictions about bimodal/unimodal cells and frequency relationships (C90-C92, C113). OpenEval supports these as logical predictions following from model mechanisms. Peer reviewer explicitly endorses these predictions as interesting to experimentalists and requests they be listed prominently.

Both evaluate asymmetric suppression mechanism producing bimodal/unimodal firing patterns (C9, C34-C35, C52, C61-C64). OpenEval finds the mechanism well-explained and supported. Peer reviewer also supports this, with Reviewer 1 calling it especially interesting and Reviewer 2 praising the model's explanatory power.

Both address phase shift mechanism and theta sweeps (C7-C8, C32-C33). OpenEval finds the analytical derivation and simulations clearly demonstrate the mechanism. Peer reviewer strongly supports this as the main result with 'convincing evidence' and 'surprisingly large explanatory power.'

Both evaluate connection between model dynamics and experimental theta sweeps (C5-C6, C30, C46). OpenEval supports the qualitative match to experimental patterns. Peer reviewer also supports this as part of the main result, with all three reviewers endorsing the forward and backward sequences.

Both address theta frequency oscillations (C44-C45). OpenEval supports that oscillation frequency can be tuned to theta range. Peer reviewer expresses uncertainty about robustness, questioning sensitivity to parameter variations and noting lack of evidence for external pacemaker driving theta band oscillations.

Both evaluate model architecture and oscillatory tracking mechanism (C28-C29). OpenEval finds the mathematical formulations and simulations clearly demonstrate the mechanism. Peer reviewer strongly supports this, praising the 'simple yet rather illuminating competition between internally driven and externally driven dynamical trends.'

Both address intrinsic mobility and internally generated dynamics (C27, C38). OpenEval supports the theoretical analysis and validation. Peer reviewer explicitly describes the internally generated traveling-wave dynamics as a key strength of the model.

Both evaluate predictions about asymmetric bump heights (C56-C58). OpenEval supports these as demonstrated predictions. Peer reviewer explicitly endorses this prediction as especially interesting to experimentalists and requests it be listed prominently.

Both address 2D extension (C111). OpenEval supports this as a reasonable extrapolation with preliminary results. Peer reviewer implicitly accepts this straightforward extension through lack of challenge.

OpenEval evaluates background claims about experimental literature and knowledge gaps (C1-C4, C13-C24) as well-supported and providing appropriate motivation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background/motivation claims.

OpenEval rates the laminar difference explanation (C65-C66) as uncertain and speculative, requiring experimental validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific claim about layer-specific adaptation.

OpenEval supports the comparison to existing models (C93-C101) as fair and well-documented, with novel contributions clearly articulated. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing the model comparison claims.

OpenEval rates grid cell extension and coordination hypothesis (C115-C117) as uncertain, noting it's presented as future direction without implementation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these grid cell claims.

OpenEval supports claims about functional significance of phase precession (C74-C75) as accurately representing prior work. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these functional context claims.

OpenEval supports the cyclical sweep length prediction (C114) as clearly demonstrated and testable. Peer reviewer R3 mentions this pattern should be 'remarked upon' but doesn't provide separate evaluation; OpenEval treats it as distinct prediction.
